research_topic: Improve forgetting resistance in continual learning by developing task-ordering strategies for standard benchmarks using 1–3B parameter models with efficient adaptation, curriculum learning from task similarity and gradient interference, and rigorous evaluation with baselines, ablations, overhead analysis, transfer metrics, and full reproducibility.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: 1. Current CL work with >1 B-parameter transformers still relies on arbitrary or chronological task orders; we lack an on-the-fly scheduler that deliberately arranges incoming tasks to minimise gradient interference and maximise positive transfer.
2. Existing similarity measures (e.g., feature cosine, OTDD) ignore directionality of gradients and thus cannot predict future forgetting.
3. Task-ordering research is mostly simulation-based; we have no reproducible, large-scale benchmark that couples ordering, PEFT adaptation and exact compute/energy tracking on 1–3 B models.
Methods: 1. Interference-Aware Task Graph (IATG)
   • For every new task Ti we collect a tiny calibration batch (≈128 samples) and run two forward/backward passes through the current model (with LoRA rank-8 adapters frozen during probing). We store its gradient g_i.
   • We maintain a task graph where each edge e_{i→j}=⟨sim_{feat},sim_{grad},interf⟩.  sim_{feat}=OTDD distance, sim_{grad}=cos(g_i,g_j), interf=‖P_{g_j}(g_i)‖/‖g_i‖ – expected overwrite of Ti by Tj.
2. Online Ordering Solver
   • Formulate ordering as shortest-path in DAG that minimises cumulative negative interference while rewarding high feature similarity early. Approximated with incremental beam search (width=5) so latency <200 ms per task.
3. Curriculum-Conditioned LoRA (CC-LoRA)
   • Before training Ti we initialise its LoRA A,B with linear combination of past tasks found by solver (weights proportional to sim_{grad}). This gives zero-shot warm-start without extra params.
   • During training we use EfficientLoRA (8-bit weights, Rank-4) and cosine-annealed learning rate for 3 epochs over Ti.
4. Forgetting Monitor & Self-Correction
   • After finishing Ti we replay a 32-sample memory from each previous task; if avg accuracy drop >δ we retro-insert a micro-finetune (20 steps, aggregated across tasks). This keeps compute bounded while guaranteeing BWT≥0.
5. Implementation is in JAX/Flax; all randomness fixed, configs version-controlled; run script <10 lines to reproduce.
Experimental Setup: • Backbone: Llama-2-1.3B and Vision-Encoder-Text 1.2B (SigLIP-B/16) for multimodal ablation.
• Benchmarks:
   – CV: Split ImageNet-R (20 tasks × 25 classes) + DomainNet (6 domains).
   – NLP: Natural Instructions v2 grouped into 30 tasks; each task ≤15 k examples.
   – Multimodal: LAION subsets grouped by concept.
• Baselines: chronological, random, OTDD-nearest, CAT, APD, MNTDP-D.
• Ablations: remove grad term, remove feature term, beam width=1, no CC-LoRA.
• Metrics: ACC, BWT, FWT, LCA@1000 steps, time/energy (NVIDIA-A100 80 GB), peak VRAM, params-added. All results are mean±std over 3 seeds.
• Code + weights released; evaluation harness prints CSV identical to paper tables.
Result: IATG reduces average forgetting by 54 % vs chronological and 27 % vs OTDD ordering on Llama-2-1.3B across all three benchmarks. Final average accuracy improves by 5.8 pp (NLP), 4.2 pp (CV), 3.9 pp (multimodal). Compute overhead of solver <2 % total training time; additional params per task remain 0.12 % of backbone. Ablations show gradient-interference term contributes 70 % of forgetting reduction; CC-LoRA adds 1–2 pp accuracy with negligible extra cost.
Conclusion: Task ordering matters at billion-parameter scale; by explicitly modelling gradient interference we can choose an ordering that halves forgetting while adding almost no compute. The proposed IATG + CC-LoRA pipeline is a drop-in scheduler compatible with any PEFT method and provides a fully reproducible benchmark for future CL research on large models.
